Overall, a great show but the management and seating experience could definitely be better.

featured_reviews.name: Dr. Aman Bhonsle
featured_reviews.review_text:
I’ve spent a decade in Southeast Asia. I’ve seen how cultural centres work there. Not just as venues, but as ecosystems. Programming, audiences, and moderation move together. Momentum is built deliberately.

In that context, this space feels timely. Important, even.

So I walked into this short film event with my wife. Hopeful.

And credit where it’s due. The space is beautifully put together. Thoughtful. Inviting. Clearly built by people who care. The audience was tuned in.

All the right ingredients were there.

Where the evening struggled was in the films.

Several of the works felt giddy and amateur. Technically rough. Narratively unfocused. Distractingly underdeveloped.

One film had incoherent audio. Meaning became guesswork, not interpretation.

Another leaned hard into abstraction. Not out of necessity. More like a shortcut. It tried, sheepishly, to channel Lynch or Nolan but landed closer to a junky home video.

Abstraction isn’t the problem. Effort is effort.

Not every film needs to be “Inception”.

But abstraction without craft, clarity, or purpose turns into obfuscation.

The stories strained for depth instead of arriving at it. The result wasn’t mystery. It was work that felt unfinished and flat.

This isn’t the venue’s fault.

But programming work of this quality undermines both the space and the audience who has paid money to be there.

Then came the Q&A.
This is where things felt uncomfortable for me.

One filmmaker seemed drunk on his own mythology. Cocky. Dismissive. Actively discouraging questions. He spoke as if the audience owed him their attention. No respect for their presence or participation. A bad attitude. Plain and simple. He talked about not wanting to make the film. About being drunk through the conception and writing process. No self-awareness. No sense that he was poisoning the room.

It left a sour taste. Which is a shame.

A space this carefully crafted deserves better stewardship of its conversations.

Another film’s “representative” wasn’t even a filmmaker. It was a producer. Someone who hadn’t been at the shoot. Didn’t understand the technical process. Couldn’t answer basic questions.

Why seat someone like that for a Q&A?

The engagement collapsed. Limp. Unsatisfying.

I come from filmmaking and television. I expected some juice.

Back-and-forth.
War stories.
Love of the craft.
Obsession.

Instead, the interactions felt evasive. Hollow. And the films, frankly, had the roughness of poorly made student projects. Which is wild, considering how sharp even simple YouTube and Instagram reels look today.

You can’t blame everything on the venue.
But curation matters. A lot.

Not all events are created equal.

Their Instagram shows a genuine celebration of life and creativity. That’s why I’m willing to believe this was a one-off misstep. Still, it was our first experience of the space.

There were smaller issues too.

The welcome could’ve been warmer. If there’s an event, don’t leave people outside like they’re waiting for a bus. A few extra chairs wouldn’t hurt.

No water. No tea. No snacks.

An odd hosting choice—though the upcoming café sounds promising.

This is a new space. It’s finding its footing.

What’s already been built is impressive.
The foundation is solid.

The trajectory is familiar to me as I’ve watched cultural districts in Osaka, Spain, Taipei, Thailand, Seoul and Singapore flourish during my visits there.

Early experimentation.
Then sharper programming.
Then confidence.

That’s the game.

I’ll return eventually.

This first visit had gaps.
But it also showed promise.

With tighter curation, stronger moderation and better audience care, this space could become a genuine cultural anchor for the city.

featured_reviews.name: Anil “AP” Passi
featured_reviews.review_text:
The Royal Opera House on Charni Road feels like a rare architectural pause in the middle of Mumbai movement. You step off a busy street lined with shops and traffic, then the building pulls you into a different pace, with a formal frontage and a sense of theatre before you even enter. That contrast between everyday Mumbai and a European style performance palace is a big part of why the place stays with you.  ￼

Exterior character and street presence

From the outside, the building reads as early 20th century grandeur: a long frontage designed for a ceremonial arrival, with a classical composition that signals performance and status. The overall language is Baroque leaning, with European styling blended with Indian detailing, which gives it an identity that fits colonial era Bombay while still feeling local.  ￼

What stands out most is the way the façade is not a single flat wall. It feels staged, like a set, with a central focus and a rhythm across the front that guides the eye towards the main entry. It is not oversized compared with modern towers, yet it has presence because the proportions are confident and the detailing is deliberate.

First impression inside: materials that signal luxury

The interiors were conceived with the intent of being lavish, and that intent is still legible today. The building is repeatedly described as having a rich interior tradition, with Italian marble, Minton tile flooring, ornate plasterwork, and painted murals within the dome areas.  ￼

Even if you are not an architecture enthusiast, these materials land immediately because they change how sound and light behave. Marble and polished surfaces carry light differently, and the decorative plasterwork softens transitions between walls and ceiling so spaces feel more ceremonial than functional.

The auditorium: the heart of the architecture

The auditorium is where the building’s architectural logic becomes clear. It is laid out as a classic proscenium theatre with tiered seating and boxes, designed for sightlines and social hierarchy at the same time. The venue capacity is around 575, spread across multiple levels, which keeps it intimate enough to feel close to the stage while still delivering a grand visual.  ￼

Key architectural moments people notice again and again:
•	Royal boxes and balcony tiers that frame the room and make the audience part of the spectacle  ￼
•	Dome and ceiling artwork that draws your gaze upward and makes the room feel taller and more ceremonial  ￼
•	Chandeliers that act as centrepiece objects rather than just lighting, including pieces associated with the Sassoon mansion Sans Souci  ￼

There is also an architectural intelligence in the way theatres manage sound. Sources describing the venue highlight design attention to performance needs across the hall and backstage areas, reflecting a building intended to function as a modern venue while keeping its historic form.  ￼

Restoration work: why it matters to the experience

A lot of the enjoyment here comes from the fact that you are seeing a restored heritage venue rather than a replica. The Royal Opera House reopened in 2016 after a long restoration period, with conservation work led by Abha Narain Lambah and Associates, and it has become a reference point for how a privately owned heritage building can return to active cultural use.  ￼

You can feel that restoration approach in the way surfaces look cared for without looking brand new. The building does not try to hide its age, but it avoids the dusty museum effect by keeping the spaces active and performance ready.

featured_reviews.review_text:
Attended their 8pm show tonight. It was largely funny and entertaining. Kudos to the performers! Just a couple of points:

1. I was laughing loudly at the first stand up comedian's act, but being a yogi, I sometimes enter silent spaces within myself- so was quieter after a while, within his performance. And the stand up comic started picking on me in a big way. He asked me if I was okay because I wasn't laughing- I told him, I am okay, its just that I am a yogi so I become quiet after a while. He just thought that I i didn't like his act and kept commenting on the yogic posture I was sitting in, my shawl, saying that I have 'south mumbai' confidence in a derogatory way, started making jokes indirectly about me. Then I also pushed back and told him that he was making some offensive jokes about handicapped people etc. I did get that he was just trying to be funny- but he just woudn't stop picking on me- though, I was laughing at all his jokes largely. Its one thing to engage and interact with your audience- its another to be downright offensive- specially when the stand up comic himself can't take the pushback from us. I am a yogi-so I didn't let this disturb me- but this is not how an entertaining night should be. He ended his act by saying that his friend who did Vipassana (the silence program) can't stop talking about it and how its an oxymoron. See, you are totally entitled to your opinion- but sometimes comics will just keep pushing and pushing the audience members, though they have paid for your program and are there for a happy evening out. In fact the comic said to me that I was messing with the audience's good time this evening- because I pointed out that some of his jokes were offensive- which I did only because he wouldn't stop throwing his jibes at me. I think that you guys can do better than this please.

2. The stand up comedians displayed on their poster on bookmyshow- are very popular, well known names- none of whom were there tonight. It is mentioned on their poster in a not very legible font that the final lineup may or maynot feature those popular comics. But that is a very very easy to miss point- on their poster. However, most comics tonight were still good and the show was entertaining overall

I wish them the very best for their endevours!
